extracted.intended_audience: financial economists, corporate governance researchers, securities regulators, and policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical procedure and robustness checks for decomposing firms' total market-value losses following discovery of financial misrepresentation into fines, class-action settlements, accounting readjustments, and residual (reputation) losses. Includes data/sample requirements, alternative estimation methods, and cross-sectional regression specifications for determinants of reputation loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation Loss decomposition formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation Loss = ΔVt − (Fine Effect + Class-Action Effect + Readjustment Effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ΔVt is the abnormal loss in firm value (the Total Dollar Loss). The Reputation Loss is measured as the residual after removing the portions attributable to investors' expectations of monetary sanctions (fines and class-action settlements) and the readjustment effect (market revaluation from corrected accounting items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fine Effect (monetary sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fine effect reflects the portion of share value loss attributable to investors' expectations of future monetary sanctions against the firm — the aggregate amount of all monetary fines, including penalties and disgorgement, eventually levied against the firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimates are the sums of all monetary fines imposed on the firm. In practice the authors sum fines/penalties from regulatory and private actions; when estimating readjustment/charge-offs they remove monetary penalties from net charge-offs to avoid double counting. Note: the paper uses nominal penalty figures (not discounted or after-tax), which may understate or otherwise affect comparisons with reputation loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-Action Effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The portion of share value loss attributable to investors' expectations of private class-action lawsuits and settlements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculated as the aggregate class-action awards/settlements imposed on the firm (included with monetary sanctions when partitioning total loss). The paper sums class-action settlements net of any proceeds that should not be double-counted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readjustment Effect — asset-based estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: The readjustment effect is calculated by adding special items, accounting charges, and charge-offs (Compustat items #17, #183, and #349) and then multiplying by the industry median market-to-book assets ratio using two-digit SIC codes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors select the largest single-year write-off during the enforcement period (from last year of violation through resolution) and multiply by the industry median market-to-book multiple. For banks/financial firms include net charge-offs (item #349) but remove monetary penalties to avoid double counting. This asset-based approach is used as the primary (conservative) estimate of the readjustment effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readjustment Effect — earnings-based alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative readjustment estimate: subtract restated net income from originally reported income (summed over all restated periods) and multiply the earnings change by the median industry price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method requires access to 10-K/10-Q/8-K filings (EDGAR) and careful matching of restatements to the enforcement action. The authors restrict this approach to violations beginning after May 6, 1996 (EDGAR coverage) and manually verify restatements are related to the enforcement action. The earnings-based approach often yields smaller readjustment estimates than the asset-based approach in their sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational-expectations assumption underpinning decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a rational expectations assumption, the sizes of the actual fines, class-action settlements, and readjustments are unbiased estimates of investors' expectations of these amounts when news becomes public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption justifies treating observed monetary sanctions and readjustments as the components investors anticipated and therefore as subtractable from total abnormal value loss to infer reputation loss. The paper notes sensitivity to this assumption but adopts it throughout the decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partition Total Dollar Loss into components
rubrics_metrics.description: The Total Dollar Loss (change in market capitalization due to announcements related to the misconduct) is partitioned into: Fine Effect, Class-Action Effect, Readjustment Effect, and Reputation Loss (residual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report aggregate, mean, and median dollar losses and compute each component's share of total loss 'based on means' and 'based on medians' (as in Table 9). This partitioning is the central reporting framework for results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data and sample coverage requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use firms listed on CRSP and Compustat for valuation and accounting items; use EDGAR/SEC filings for restatement/earnings-based methods; sample of enforcement actions from regulators (SEC/DOJ) over the chosen period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors analyze enforcement actions initiated from 1978–2002 tracked through Nov 15, 2005. For earnings-based readjustment estimates they restrict the sample to violation periods starting after May 6, 1996 to ensure EDGAR access. CRSP/Compustat coverage is required to compute market and accounting measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of negative reputation-loss estimates (censoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some individual measures of reputation loss can be negative; to avoid treating these as reputation-enhancing events, negative reputation losses are set to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this left-censoring at zero, the authors estimate Tobit regressions (with left censoring set at zero) when modeling reputation loss across firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-sectional determinants/regressors for reputation loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Include measures of a firm's reliance on implicit contracts and financial condition as regressors: R&D flag (R&D>0), High intangible assets flag (intangibles/assets > 0.25), log market-to-book ratio, Financial distress flag (bankruptcy), Leverage ratio (liabilities/assets), plus controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control variables include: log market capitalization (size), log firm age (months on CRSP), free cash flow (NI + depreciation / assets), top executive named flag, fraud flag, company named flag, log of individual penalties, # days in enforcement period, violation period cumulative abnormal return (stock run-up), and incomplete enforcement action flag. Expected signs: e.g., reputation loss positively related to R&D and intangibles; leverage and financial distress may increase reputation loss (ambiguous theory but positive in results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent variable / model specification choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Two model specifications: Model 1 uses Reputation Loss as a fraction of Total Dollar Loss; Model 2 uses the natural logarithm of the dollar Reputation Loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate Tobit cross-sectional regressions for the full sample (N=384). Evaluate goodness-of-fit (χ2), report p-values and coefficient significance. Sensitivity to model specification is addressed in robustness checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and sensitivity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct sensitivity tests to probe robustness of reputation-loss estimates to alternative readjustment calculations, sample restrictions, and extreme assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: recalc readjustment assuming a common market-to-book ratio for all firms, include all write-offs over the entire enforcement period, use earnings-based readjustment instead of asset-based, arbitrarily inflate readjustment estimates, and restrict sample to firms that survive enforcement. The main conclusion (reputation loss large relative to legal penalties) is robust across these checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for delisting and unresolved enforcement-action bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Delisted or failed firms and unresolved enforcement actions lead to understated dollar-loss estimates because returns are unobservable for non-trading periods; unresolved actions may miss restatements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that 190 of 384 firms in Panel A failed or delisted during enforcement. To check bias, they restrict analysis to surviving firms (Panel B) and find even larger reputation-loss shares. Also drop firms with incomplete enforcement actions when computing earnings-based readjustment estimates to avoid understatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asset-based write-off selection details
rubrics_metrics.description: For the asset-based readjustment effect, determine the book value of assets written off during each year of the enforcement period and select the largest single-year write-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiply that write-off by the industry median market-to-book ratio (two-digit SIC) to estimate market-value inflation from misreporting. This approach is argued to be practical given diverse restatement formats and stealth restatements by firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnings-based readjustment implementation details
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the earnings-based method, compute the sum over all years of the violation and enforcement period of the firm's earnings change (original minus restated) and multiply by the median industry P/E multiple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify restatements by examining 10-K, 10-Q, and 8-K filings and match reasons for restatement to enforcement action causes. Use contemporaneous median industry P/E computed from Compustat (item #199 divided by item #58). This method may be constrained by missing filings and stealth restatements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative assessment of asset- versus earnings-based methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Asset-based estimates of the readjustment effect tend to be larger (and thus yield more conservative reputation-loss estimates) than earnings-based estimates in the authors' sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports mean and median comparisons for a 47-firm subsample: asset-based mean/median readjustment ($369.94m / $9.14m) vs earnings-based ($192.91m / $4.35m). The authors prefer the asset-based approach for practical reasons (inconsistent restatement formats, stealth restatements) while acknowledging conceptual arguments that may favor price-to-book measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and reporting of legal-penalty timing and payment realities
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper uses nominal (undiscounted) penalty and settlement figures and does not adjust for after-tax effects, potential later reductions, bankruptcy, or insurance reimbursements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors acknowledge that omitting discounting and after-tax adjustments may understate the relative size of legal penalties and therefore bias their decomposition toward larger measured reputation losses. They discuss these limitations and note that observed reputation losses remain large even under conservative adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation metrics and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Report results as aggregate dollar amounts, means, medians, and percentages of the Total Dollar Loss; interpret reputation loss as present value of expected higher financing costs and diminished cash flows after discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative interpretation: for every $1 of inflated market value from deception, the firm loses the $1 plus additional amounts due to legal penalties and reputation (paper finds ~ $0.36 legal + $2.71 reputation on average; larger for surviving firms). Use both mean- and median-based percentage breakdowns to address skewness.
